title: Determine which restoration pathway fits your family history
description: Article 116(2) Basic Law: for descendants of Germans persecuted between 1933 and 1945 (most commonly German Jews). StAG §15: for descendants of those barred from citizenship by historic discriminatory laws (pre-1953 maternal-line cases, pre-1993 out-of-wedlock paternal-line cases, etc.). Both routes are free, no language test, no residency required, and allow dual citizenship.

title: Identify the persecuted or excluded German ancestor
description: For Article 116: an ancestor who held German citizenship and lost it between 1933-01-30 and 1945-05-08 for racial, religious, or political reasons. Most commonly: German Jews stripped of citizenship by the 1941 11th Reich Citizenship Ordinance, including those who emigrated and 'lost' citizenship under various Nazi decrees.

title: Map the documentary chain from you to the German ancestor
description: Each generation needs: birth certificate; marriage certificate where surnames change; death certificate. Note any gaps — those are your acquisition targets. Document any name changes (Schmidt → Smith) that will need affidavit explanation.

title: Order your German ancestor's birth certificate (Geburtsurkunde) from the Standesamt
description: Each German town has a Standesamt (civil registry). For Jewish ancestors with pre-1875 records, look to synagogue records via Leo Baeck Institute, Yad Vashem, or LDS FamilySearch. Pre-1945 East German records are often held by the federal archives (Bundesarchiv).

links.label: Leo Baeck Institute — German Jewish history

title: Document evidence of German citizenship before persecution
description: Pre-1941 German passport, Heimatschein, residence registration (Meldekarte), military service book, or birth registration in Germany. The German consulate provides a list of acceptable evidence.

title: Document evidence of persecution between 1933 and 1945
description: Listing in the 1941 Reichsanzeiger (expatriation gazette) is the gold standard. Other evidence: emigration after 1933 to a country of refuge, Yad Vashem testimony, naturalization records in country of refuge that note prior German nationality, restitution claims under post-war German laws (BEG, BRüG).

links.label: Yad Vashem — central database of Shoah victims' names

title: Order vital records for every generation in the chain (long-form)
description: Birth, marriage, death certificates between you and the German ancestor. Long-form (with parents' names). Each US document needs an apostille from the issuing state's Secretary of State.

title: Have US documents apostilled
description: Germany is a Hague Apostille party; each US Secretary of State office issues apostilles for state-issued documents. Federal documents (FBI checks, naturalization records) go through the US Department of State authentication office.

title: Get certified German translations for any documents not in German
description: Translations must be done by a translator listed as ermächtigt/öffentlich bestellt by a German state (Bundesland). Translations done abroad must be apostilled to be accepted in Germany.

title: Complete the Bundesverwaltungsamt restoration application
description: Article 116 uses BVA-Antrag StAG-A; StAG §15 uses BVA-Antrag StAG-B. Download the current form from the BVA website. The form covers you and any minor children — adults must file separately.

title: Submit the application directly to the BVA in Cologne
description: The application can be submitted directly by mail to the Bundesverwaltungsamt, Postfach 68 06 65, 50728 Köln, Germany. You do NOT need to use a consulate (and skipping the consulate is often faster). No fee.

title: Wait for BVA processing
description: Current processing times for Article 116 and StAG §15 are 18–36 months, with significant backlog from increased applications. The BVA will request additional documents by mail if needed; respond promptly.

title: Receive your Einbürgerungsurkunde (Certificate of Naturalization / Restoration)
description: This is your official proof of German citizenship. It is the foundation document for your German passport application. Keep multiple certified copies.

title: Apply for a German passport (Reisepass) at a German consulate
description: After receiving your citizenship certificate, schedule an appointment at the German consulate with jurisdiction over your residence. Fee approximately €82. The German passport is a full EU passport.

title: Understand your dual-citizen status and tax obligations
description: Germany has allowed dual citizenship since 2024 (and restoration cases have always allowed it). The US taxes citizens on worldwide income; Germany taxes residents. The US-Germany tax treaty handles most overlap, but consult a cross-border CPA before relocating.

title: If you have children, file restoration applications for them too
description: Minor children can be included on a parent's application. Adult children must file their own Article 116 or StAG §15 application referencing the same ancestor — this is much faster than a fresh case since the BVA already has the ancestor file.
